title: Shoulder replacement: when is it needed, and what is a reverse shoulder replacement?
seoTitle: Shoulder Replacement & Reverse Shoulder: When It's Needed
metaDescription: When shoulder replacement makes sense, how a reverse shoulder replacement differs, what recovery involves, how long implants last, and when not to operate.
intro: Most painful shoulders never need a replacement. But when arthritis or a badly damaged rotator cuff takes away sleep and the ability to lift a cup or comb your hair, and other treatment has stopped helping, a new joint is a reasonable option to discuss. This guide explains the main types, including the reverse shoulder replacement, and what recovery honestly looks like.
summary: Shoulder replacement is considered when arthritis, an irreparable rotator cuff with arthritis (cuff tear arthropathy), or a complex fracture in an older adult causes pain and loss of function that non-surgical care has not relieved. A reverse replacement swaps the ball and socket so the deltoid muscle can lift the arm when the rotator cuff no longer works.

sections.heading: When does a shoulder actually need replacing?
sections.body: A replacement is considered when the joint surface is worn or broken beyond repair and pain or stiffness is limiting daily life despite proper non-surgical treatment. The usual reasons are osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, cuff tear arthropathy, and some complex upper-arm (proximal humerus) fractures in older adults. An X-ray showing arthritis is not, on its own, a reason to operate. AAOS OrthoInfo lists the conditions where a reverse replacement may be considered: shoulder arthritis with a damaged rotator cuff, an irreparable rotator cuff tear, complex fractures, chronic dislocation, failed earlier shoulder surgery or replacement, and tumours. It also notes surgery may be recommended when nonsurgical treatments have not relieved pain.
bullets: Pain at night or at rest that disturbs sleep
Difficulty with dressing, washing hair, reaching a shelf
Arthritis or bone damage confirmed on X-ray or CT
Months of physiotherapy, medicines and activity changes without enough relief

sections.heading: What should be tried before surgery?
sections.body: Non-surgical care comes first for arthritis and most cuff problems: activity changes, a structured physiotherapy programme, pain relief that suits your kidneys and stomach, and sometimes a steroid injection for a flare. Many people manage well this way for years. Fractures are different, because the decision is made in the first days after injury. Many fractures of the upper arm in older adults heal acceptably in a sling without surgery. A replacement is usually reserved for fractures where the head of the bone is shattered or its blood supply is likely lost. If a fracture happened after a minor fall, it is also worth checking bone strength. See our guide on osteoporosis and fracture prevention.

sections.heading: Anatomic, reverse or hemiarthroplasty: which suits whom?
sections.body: The choice depends mainly on whether the rotator cuff still works. An anatomic total replacement copies the normal ball-and-socket and needs a healthy cuff. A reverse replacement puts the ball on the socket side and the cup on the arm bone, so the deltoid can power the arm without the cuff. A hemiarthroplasty replaces only the ball and is now used more selectively.

sections.heading: What is recovery like?
sections.body: Expect a sling for several weeks, early gentle exercises guided by a physiotherapist, and gradual improvement over many months rather than weeks. Royal Berkshire NHS Foundation Trust's discharge advice for total shoulder replacement describes a sling for 3 to 6 weeks, driving usually after about 6 to 8 weeks when safe, light work from about 6 weeks, heavy lifting from about 3 months, and strength and movement continuing to improve for up to 18 months. AAOS OrthoInfo advises, after reverse replacement, avoiding extreme arm positions and not lifting more than about 5 lb (roughly 2 kg) for the first 6 weeks unless your surgeon says otherwise. Your own surgeon's protocol may differ.
bullets: Most people can feed, dress and groom themselves within days, according to OrthoInfo
Lifting the arm forward and pain relief usually improve the most
Turning the arm outward and reaching behind the back often return less fully, particularly after a reverse replacement
Do not push up from a chair with the operated arm in the early weeks

sections.heading: How long does a shoulder replacement last?
sections.body: Most shoulder replacements last more than ten years. An NIHR summary of a 2020 Lancet Rheumatology review (Evans and colleagues), combining case series and national joint registry reports, found about 92 to 95% of total shoulder replacements, about 94% of reverse replacements and about 86 to 90% of partial replacements were still working (had not needed revision) at 10 years. Evidence beyond 10 years, particularly for reverse replacements, is more limited, because few studies have followed patients for 15 to 20 years.

sections.heading: What are the risks, and when should you not operate?
sections.body: Shoulder replacement is major surgery. OrthoInfo lists infection, bleeding and nerve injury, and implant problems such as wear, loosening, fracture around the implant and dislocation, any of which may need further surgery. Surgery is usually not advised while there is active infection, when the deltoid muscle or its nerve does not work, when medical conditions make anaesthesia unsafe, or when symptoms are mild enough to manage without it. If pain is mainly from a frozen shoulder or a repairable rotator cuff tear, replacement is not the answer.
bullets: Fever, or a wound that becomes red, hot, swollen or leaks fluid
New numbness, tingling or weakness in the hand or arm after the nerve block has worn off
A sudden clunk, deformity or sharp loss of movement (possible dislocation)
Calf swelling, chest pain or breathlessness

faqs.q: Is a reverse shoulder replacement only for older people?
faqs.a: It is used most often in older adults with cuff tear arthropathy or complex fractures, because it does not rely on the rotator cuff. Long-term data in younger patients are more limited, so the decision is made carefully.

faqs.q: Will I be able to lift my arm above my head?
faqs.a: Lifting the arm forward usually improves a lot, especially after a reverse replacement, but reaching behind the back and turning the arm outward may stay limited.

faqs.q: How long before I can drive?
faqs.a: NHS discharge advice for total shoulder replacement suggests driving is usually possible after about 6 to 8 weeks, once you are out of the sling and can control the car safely.

faqs.q: How long will the new joint last?
faqs.a: A 2020 review of registry and case series data found most total and reverse replacements were still working at 10 years, with partial replacements doing slightly less well.

faqs.q: When should I call my doctor after surgery?
faqs.a: Call promptly for fever, a red or leaking wound, new numbness or weakness in the hand, a sudden clunk or loss of movement, or calf swelling or breathlessness.
